newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa may retain some forex controls - Manuel.
newsitem.headline: South Africa may retain some forex controls - Manuel.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Tuesday the country might in future retain a "modicum" of foreign exchange controls.

"What the end product is at this stage is still up in the air. Will we retain a modicum of control as in Chile or would you go the Mexican route, has not finally been settled," Manuel said at a news briefing in Cape Town.

President Nelson Mandela's government has previously promised the eventual lifting of exchange controls on residents, but has not spelt out a timetable. There have been growing calls for clarification on the issue in the face of the plunging rand.
Manuel said there was no final deadline for the lifting of exchange controls, adding further moves would hinge on the country's foreign reserves.
"It's not about policy. It is tied into your reserve position at any given time. If you have a high level of reserves I think you have more manoeuverability," he said.
"If you've got the cushion of reserves it does make a very, very substantial difference."
South Africa's foreign exchange reserves stood at 10 billion rand at the end of September -- equivalent to four weeks import cover -- and are expected to have slipped further in October.
October reserves data is due for release on Thursday.
Manuel said an International Monetary Fund (IMF) facility remained an option for South Africa but the government was not currently in discussion on an IMF loan.
"We remain in discussion with the Reserve Bank. The finger is on the pulse. But I'm not suggesting we are in discussion with the IMF about the standby facility," he said.
Manuel said the IMF should be seen as lender of last resort and the Reserve Bank still had credit lines available to it.
"The Reserve Bank has something in the order of 15 to 17 billion rand of lines," Manuel said.
Under IMF rules, South Africa would be able to draw up to 100 percent of its IMF quota -- or some $2 billion -- for use as a standby or extended fund facility.
